title: How Sign Language Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss sign language, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article by Jonathan Strickland. They cover the historical mistreatment of deaf people, the founding of Martha's Vineyard Sign Language, the role of Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and Laurent Clerc in founding the American School for the Deaf, and Gallaudet University. They explain American Sign Language (ASL) grammar, including phonology, morphology, topic-comment structure, tense marked by space and time signs, non-manual markers, and fingerspelling. They discuss sign language etiquette, a fake interpreter at Mandela's memorial, DC government interpreters, and sign systems such as Signed Exact English, Pidgin Signed English, and International Sign. They close with baby sign language and a listener mail request about HIV.

segments.title: Opening banter about the article
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and praise Jonathan Strickland's HowStuffWorks article on sign language, noting there are hundreds of sign languages and that the article focuses on American Sign Language.

segments.title: Historical mistreatment of deaf people
segments.summary: The hosts describe how deaf people were historically mistreated, including restrictions in Torah temple rituals, denial of education by ancient Greeks, and St. Augustine's view. Education efforts began around the Renaissance, and deaf communities developed their own sign languages.
topics: deaf community origins of sign language

segments.title: Martha's Vineyard Sign Language
segments.summary: Because of hereditary deafness in an isolated community founded by English settlers, up to a quarter of Martha's Vineyard residents were deaf. Martha's Vineyard Sign Language developed, was used widely, and became extinct when the last deaf resident died in 1952. Oliver Sacks reported that some elders signed while speaking.

segments.title: Founding of American deaf education
segments.summary: Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet traveled to France, learned from Abbe Sicard, and with Laurent Clerc founded the American School for the Deaf in 1817 in Hartford, Connecticut. The school blended French and existing American practices. Gallaudet University and its football team, the Bison, are mentioned.
topics: French Sign Language origins of ASL

segments.title: ASL linguistics: phonology and morphology
segments.summary: The hosts explain that ASL has its own grammar, syntax, and phonology, with a discrete set of handshapes and movements rather than a distinct sign for every word. Morphology describes how hand movements form concepts. ASL does not follow English syntax.

segments.title: Iconic signs, facial expression, and sign modification
segments.summary: Examples include signing deer and moose, and the importance of facial expression, body language, and use of space. Signs for verbs and nouns differ in size, and the same sign can change meaning depending on how it is delivered, such as eat and food. The Mandela memorial fake interpreter is described, and his lack of facial expression is noted as a giveaway.

segments.title: Fingerspelling, neologisms, and tense in ASL
segments.summary: Fingerspelling is used for names and specific concepts, and spatial reference points are set up for people not present. New signs are created for terms like fiscal cliff, with prescriptive and descriptive views. Tense is set by a time sign at the start, and space indicates recent or distant events. Directional verbs such as give show subject and object.

segments.title: Sign language etiquette
segments.summary: Etiquette includes waiting for the signer to finish and look up before responding, not interrupting, keeping attention on the signer when they address an imaginary person, and walking around rather than between signers. Interpreters in DC are discussed, including the air guitar term for uncertified interpreters.

segments.title: Other sign systems and baby sign language
segments.summary: Signed Exact English, Pidgin Signed English, and International Sign (Gestuno) are described, along with the debate over immersion education. Baby sign language is discussed, with claims that it may help speech development. The hosts then move to listener mail about HIV and a possible future episode.
